 Juneau heating aid applications open under different rules
 Published 1:30 pm Friday, November 13, 2026
 By Jeffrey Kennett Juneau Empire Staff 
 Tlingit-Haida Regional Housing Authority in Juneau is accepting applications for its 2027 heating assistance program from eligible older residents and people with disabilities. (Michael Penn/Juneau Empire file photo)
 Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... 
 As winter heating bills arrive in Juneau, residents looking for help with fuel or electricity costs have two assistance programs to navigate. Eligibility depends partly on tribal citizenship, and applying through the wrong agency could delay financial relief.
 Tlingit-Haida Regional Housing Authority began accepting applications for its 2027 Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program on Nov. 1 from eligible residents who are 60 or older or have qualifying disabilities. Other eligible households can begin applying Dec. 1, with the application period scheduled to continue through June 30, 2027.
 For Juneau and Douglas residents, the authority’s program is limited to eligible tribal citizen households. Other residents generally seek assistance through Alaska’s Division of Public Assistance, which opened its heating assistance season Oct. 1.
 According to the city’s Commission on Sustainability, space heating accounts for about 21% of local energy consumption, with residents using both fossil fuels and electricity to heat their homes.
 Different income limits 
 Although both assistance systems help low-income households cover heating expenses, their eligibility rules are different.
 THRHA’s federally funded program uses an income threshold of 150% of Alaska’s federal poverty guidelines. For the current application season, a single person must have a gross monthly income of no more than $2,494, while the limit for a four-person household is $5,157. Income is generally measured using the month before an application, meaning recent earnings and changes in employment can affect eligibility.
 The state’s system includes two separate sources of assistance. Federal LIHEAP funding covers households earning up to 150% of the poverty guidelines, while the state-funded Alaska Affordable Heating Program serves qualifying households earning above 150% and up to 225%.
 Under the state’s combined 2026-27 guidelines, the upper monthly income limit is $3,739 for a single-person household and $7,733 for a family of four. Those higher figures reflect Alaska’s additional state-funded program, rather than an expansion of federal LIHEAP eligibility.
 State applicants must have at least $200 in annual out-of-pocket heating expenses, and the amount awarded depends on household income, the number of residents, the type of home and the primary heating source. For those who qualify, assistance is generally issued as a one-time payment to an approved heating fuel or electric utility provider.
 THRHA follows a similar approach, although households that heat with oil must put at least half their assistance toward oil costs. The remaining amount can be used for electricity or propane if residents provide the corresponding utility bill.
 Applications and waiting periods 
 THRHA applicants must provide proof of household income and copies of their heating or electricity bills. Those receiving Social Security or other benefits must also submit documentation showing those payments.
 For those whose heating costs are included in their rent, THRHA requires a lease agreement and rent receipt. Those living in subsidized housing may face additional eligibility requirements depending on how their utility costs are paid.
 Once all required documents are submitted, the housing authority says applications will be processed within 45 days. Its online application system is currently undergoing maintenance, so residents must download a form and submit it by email, fax or mail.
 Alaska’s Division of Public Assistance similarly advises applicants that processing a completed request may take up to 45 days. State officials recommend continuing to pay utility bills while awaiting a decision and contacting providers about payment arrangements when accounts become overdue.
 Households facing an urgent heating emergency may qualify for the state’s crisis assistance program if they have run out of fuel or expect to run out within 48 hours. Help may also be available to residents whose heating or electricity has been shut off or is at risk of disconnection.
 Applications for the state’s regular heating assistance program are accepted through April 30, while crisis assistance applications can be submitted through June 30.
 During federal fiscal year 2024, the state-administered LIHEAP program served 5,264 households, according to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, estimating that 50,440 Alaska households met its state income-eligibility criteria.
 Those figures do not provide a complete accounting of assistance across Alaska, as the federal report specifically excludes households served by 13 tribal LIHEAP administrators, which operate separately from the state’s program.
 For residents seeking assistance now, THRHA accepts applications at its office at 5446 Jenkins Drive in Juneau. Residents can also call 907-780-6868 or email energy@thrha.org for information about the tribal program. State applications are available through the Alaska Connect online portal, with assistance available by calling the Division of Public Assistance at 1-800-478-7778.
 Both organizations encourage applicants to submit complete documentation to avoid delays in processing their requests.
